newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Primakov out of action after operation.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Primakov out of action after operation.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov underwent a gallstone operation on Friday and might be out of action for up to three weeks during a crucial period in the preparation of a Russia-NATO accord.
"We hope that in two or three weeks he will be able to return to work," Professor Vitaly Bashilov, who conducted the operation at the elite central Clinical Hospital, told Reuters by telephone.
"It was a rather complicated operation and the patient's condition was not simple but everything will be alright."

Primakov, 66, missed a meeting with Portuguese Foreign Minister Jaime Gama earlier on Friday when he was taken to hospital with what a Foreign Ministry spokesman described as a "rather unexpected" bout of illness.

Primakov's possible absence from the political scene might hamper the preparation of an accord between the Western defence alliance and Russia which President Boris Yeltsin hopes to sign in Paris on May 27.
Yeltsin announced after talks with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Thursday that their special relationship could uncover the obstacles and allow the signing to go ahead.
But a Kremlin spokesman said intensive negotiations will be needed to make that a "reality" and the United States said an accord was far from being a certainty.
Primakov, a bulky and bespectacled former foreign intelligence chief, has been a key figure in several sessions of tough talks with Western leaders and NATO Secretary General Javier Solana.
The next talks between Primakov and Solana has been planned for the first half of May and a Russian Foreign Ministry official told Interfax news agency they had not been cancelled, at least for now.
Russia wants a binding agreement from NATO not to station new troops and weapons in new member states and is also seeking a say in the alliance's decision-making.
NATO leaders, especially the United States, are unwilling to concede so much to Moscow that prospective new members like Poland and Hungary would be consigned to "second-class" NATO participation.

Since his appointment in January 1996 to replace the liberal, West-leaning Andrei Kozyrev, Primakov has had a major impact on Russian foreign policy, giving it a more clearly-defined, nationalist focus.

He announced at the time he would give priority to relations with former Soviet republics and Yeltsin praised him last week for mediating a breakthrough in talks between Moldova and its breakaway Dnestr region.
Primakov, an Arabic speaker, has also stressed ties with the Middle East and Asia. Some experts have seen this as as "an assymetrical response" to NATO's expansion plans.
But Primakov has also been careful to develop relations with the West and has won praise from several Western leaders for his negotiating skills.
